It states no effective date, duration, condition, exemption, stay, report or delegation, so the dossier's single clause (the paragraph) is the whole operative inventory. First end: 1935-06-14, the day Senate Joint Resolution 113 (Public Resolution No. 26, 74th Congress, 49 Stat. 375, chapter 246) was approved. Section 2 of the resolution reads: 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed', with one proviso that narrows only the section 5 antitrust exemption. It names no code and no order, so it is not a naming instrument (owner ruling 2026-10-21, unnamed instruments), and under the owner's 2026-10-28 ruling a general rule ends a command only where something shows it extinguished that command. What shows it here is the text of the Act under which the order was made (48 Stat. 195, held): section 3(a) is the power to approve a code; section 3(b) makes the provisions of an approved code 'the standards of fair competition for such trade or industry' and a violation an unfair method of competition; section 3(c) gives the district courts jurisdiction to restrain violations of 'any code of fair competition approved under this title'; and section 10(b) lets the President cancel or modify 'any order, approval, license, rule, or regulation issued under this title', which shows the approval was a continuing act that the Act made binding through sections 3(b) and 3(c). The approval commands nothing of its own beyond that statutory operation, and the resolution repealed the approval power and the enforcement of codes together, with no clause preserving approved codes. The order's only operative act, making the code the enforceable standard, therefore ended on 1935-06-14. Alternatives considered and disclosed. (a) Earlier: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935 (caption and syllabus held), says at 542 'the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power'. The judgment concerned the Live Poultry Code; it names no other code, and nothing held shows it extinguished this approval on that date (no order of May 27 through June 14 touches any code). If a reviewer holds it ended every approval, the first end would be 1935-05-27; the claim uses June 14 because that is the first date on which held text removes approval and enforcement for all codes. (b) The original expiry of Title I two years after enactment (section 2(c), June 16, 1935) was displaced when the resolution amended section 2(c) to April 1, 1936; it is later than the repeal. (c) Later: EO 7076 (June 15, 1935, held APP text, page record date 1935-06-15; its held transcription omits the signature and date lines) amends all existing Title I executive orders 'so as to continue them in effect and to extend their operation ... until April 1, 1936, so far as consistent with the provisions of the National Industrial Recovery Act as amended and extended', but provides that it 'shall not be construed as an exercise by the President of any authority, or as authorizing any person or agency ... to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition, to provide for the enforcement of such codes'. Because the approval's force came through the provisions the resolution had repealed the day before, continuing it 'so far as consistent' with the Act as amended leaves it no enforceable operation; EO 7076 is therefore recorded here as a disclosed later order and is not treated as an extension or an end. Held EO 7075 (June 15, 1935) likewise refers to the trades 'heretofore subject to codes of fair competition'. The overtime provision that took effect on 1934-03-01 is a provision of the code, not a surviving command of this order.

XI NRA Codes 327. (May 30, 1934)'. Quotations are taken from the registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. EO 6730 (May 30, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) approves amendments to the Iron and Steel Industry code (approved August 19, 1933, EO 6254, held) and the code as amended, 'said revised Code incorporating said amendments to become effective on June 11, 1934, prior to which effective date the Code of Fair Competition approved August 19, 1933, shall continue in full force and effect', and then makes 'two statements'. The dossier's inventory lists only the two statements (characters 1366-2638 and 2640-3231); the operative approval paragraph (characters 0-1365) is missing and needs an inventory correction. Components: (A) approval of the amendments and the revised code, effective 1934-06-11; (B) the continuation of the 1933 code until 1934-06-11 (own-terms end that day); (C) statement 1: 'I have directed the Federal Trade Commission and the National Recovery Administration to study further and jointly the operation of the basing point system ... I have requested that the results of this study be reported to me within six months, together with any recommendations for revisions of the Code'; (D) statement 2: 'I will undertake promptly to provide, as the occasion may demand, for the election by employees in each industrial unit of representatives of their own choosing ... under the supervision of an appropriate governmental agency'. (A) and (B) could be ended on the grounds used for the plain approvals in this batch (S.J. Res. 113 section 2, 1935-06-14, and for (B) its own terms, 1934-06-11), with the approved code's text not held. (C) and (D) cannot be. Statement 1 is a direction to two agencies with a six-month report request (about 1934-11-30); under the owner's report-deadline ruling (2026-10-21) the report date is a spent fact and not an end, and nothing held records the study's completion, a report to the President, or an instrument ending the direction. The repeal of code approval and enforcement does not by its terms or by any held source reach a presidential study direction to the Federal Trade Commission, and EO 7252 (1935-12-21, held) terminates the National Recovery Administration but does not name the study. Statement 2 is an open-ended undertaking 'as the occasion may demand'. EO 6751 (June 28, 1934, held) creates the National Steel Labor Relations Board with authority in its section 3 to order and conduct elections in the iron and steel industry, and EO 7085 (June 24, 1935, held) continues that Board until July 1, 1935; these may show performance in part, but the undertaking covers 'each industrial unit', no held source says it was performed in full, withdrawn or extinguished, and neither order names EO 6730. Searches run 2026-10-29. (1) A scan of 51,237 txt, jsonl, csv, json and md files under jobs/ (skipping the derivative folders clause-drafts, claim-kit, case-bundles, claim-drafts, x1-class-engine, readiness-tracker and domesday-register, and cache, capture and pdf folders) for the code's title and for citations of this order by number.
